title.value: A Place Further Than the Universe

logline: Four high school girls embark on an Antarctic expedition together - one driven by grief over a missing mother, the others by restlessness, loneliness, and a hunger for something that actually matters.

renewal.note: The 13-episode original anime by Madhouse aired from January to March 2018 and concluded as a complete standalone story. No sequel has been produced or announced.

bollymeter.basis: MAL score of 8.50 from a large voting base; Anime News Network episode reviewers consistently praised the series for its emotional architecture, with ANN user weighted mean at 8.40 (Very Good+) and 86 votes of Masterpiece.

pull_quotes.text: It's been able to achieve its modest narrative ambitions without any trouble, and that foundation should give it plenty to build on.

seasons.review_body: Madhouse's original 2018 anime - broadcast on AT-X and Tokyo MX - is widely considered one of the finest anime of that decade. Directed by Atsuko Ishizuka and written by Jukki Hanada, the series uses the Antarctic expedition as both a literal and emotional destination. The four leads are distinct and credibly teenage; their reasons for attempting something this extreme are grounded in recognisable adolescent longing rather than fantasy. Anime News Network's episodic reviewers tracked the series' slow emotional build across 13 weeks, consistently noting how the show layers meaning into its visual design and character dynamics before delivering its most emotionally powerful episodes. The finale is among the most discussed in recent anime history. The series earned simulcast status on Crunchyroll and won the Anime of the Year award at the Crunchyroll Anime Awards in 2019.

episode_reviews.title: One Million Yen Worth of Youth
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: Mari Tamaki has lived a life of almost-adventures and abandoned dreams. When she meets Shirase Kobuchizawa, who has spent years saving a million yen to reach Antarctica, the premise snaps into focus immediately. The premiere is warm, propulsive, and confidently specific.
episode_reviews.the_moment: A million yen spilling from a bag - the most concrete expression of years of single-minded resolve any anime premiere has offered.
episode_reviews.review_body:
# A Place Further Than The Universe S1E1: "One Million Yen Worth of Youth" Review

*Spoiler-light verdict above. Full episode analysis below.*

A girl wakes from a dream where her mother tries to kill her with a wet towel. The joke is tiny, absurd, and useful. **Kimari** is already trapped inside the episode's main panic: high school is passing, adulthood is approaching, and the grand act of rebellion she can imagine is skipping school for Tokyo without a destination. This premiere understands that youth rarely begins with a clean mission statement. It begins with a bad plan, a packed bag, and the shame of turning back before the train can decide for you.

BollyAI's read: "One Million Yen Worth of Youth" works because it refuses to treat adventure as a mood. It takes Kimari's vague itch to do something and crashes it into **Kobuchizawa Shirase**'s impossible, expensive, painful objective. One girl wants motion. The other has a map.

## Youth Starts as a Bad Plan

Kimari's first concrete act is wonderfully small: she chooses Tokyo for an aimless journey. That matters. The episode does not open with a heroine who knows her calling, or even one who has a half-decent itinerary. the plan arrives as a suggestion, and the word fits the looseness of the moment. Tokyo is less a destination than a permission slip. If she goes there, she can tell herself she has broken routine. If she stays, nothing has to be admitted.

The writing is sharpest when it lets that contradiction sit. Kimari prepares to run away alone and rides away from school life, but the episode already knows she is not built for solitary rebellion. Her desire is sincere. Her execution is shaky. That is the point. The premiere catches the exact embarrassment of wanting a life-changing gesture before having the nerve, the reason, or the logistics to carry it.

That is why her later choice to help by calling the school and changing her story lands as more than a polite favor. It is a pivot from self-invention to participation. Kimari does not become braver by suddenly turning into a different person. She becomes useful. The episode's first little trick is to make usefulness feel like adventure's first honest form.

## The Million Yen Gives the Hour a Spine

The one million yen is the cleanest device in the premiere because it turns mood into pursuit. Before that, Kimari's story can drift by design. After the money appears, the hour has an object with weight, risk, and a question attached: who dropped it, and why? The search through freshmen rooms gives the middle stretch a procedural pulse, even when the dialogue grows crowded.

That crowdedness is the episode's most visible weakness. The dossier points to dense turn-taking and explanations through the middle and late sections, and the hour occasionally says aloud what a glance or pause could have carried. The early quiet stretches suggest a more confident rhythm, then the episode accelerates into information: Tokyo, the search, Antarctica, the ship. The movement is productive, but the gear changes can be heard.

Still, the money is a strong hook because it arrives as proof of intent before the episode fully explains the intent. When a character says Kobuchizawa has been working, the yen becomes labor. That distinction matters. The cash gives the Antarctica dream a physical form. Someone has saved. Someone has planned. Someone has been dismissed, and kept going anyway.

The amount also matters because it is too large to be whimsical. Kimari can daydream about Tokyo with a schoolbag and a burst of nerve. Kobuchizawa has converted her grief into savings. The premiere puts those two scales of desire next to each other and lets the contrast do the work. Kimari is afraid of wasting her youth. Kobuchizawa is afraid that everyone else will decide her mother's disappearance has already been filed away.

## Antarctica Turns Grief Into Logistics

Kobuchizawa's introduction gives the premiere its engine. Her mother wrote about Antarctica, went missing, and was never found. Kobuchizawa's answer is blunt: "So, I'm going to find her." That line gives the episode its charge. It takes grief that could have remained atmospheric and makes it practical, even ridiculous to everyone around it. She has a destination.

The power of the beat comes from how impossible it sounds inside the ordinary high-school frame. Antarctica is a word that changes the size of the show. Kimari's Tokyo idea suddenly looks like a practice swing. Kobuchizawa is playing a different sport altogether. The central skepticism is built directly into the premise: can she go there at all? The episode keeps returning to that doubt as the social weather Kobuchizawa lives under.

Her contradiction is the best thing in the hour. She urges others to come next Saturday to check the ship while explaining the disbelief and hardship she faces. That is not a speech about hope. It is a tactic. Come see the ship. Look at the thing. Let the idea stop being abstract. The writing understands that an impossible dream becomes harder to mock once it has a timetable.

That practicality keeps the missing-mother material from turning soggy. Kobuchizawa is not framed as a delicate symbol of loss. She is abrasive, focused, and prepared to make people uncomfortable. The episode gives her pain a route map, which makes her more interesting than a girl waiting to be pitied. She wants help, but she also wants witnesses. Those are different needs, and the premiere is smart enough to separate them.

## Support Arrives Before Belief

The premiere is careful about support. It does not require everyone to understand Kobuchizawa before helping her. a character explains they saw her and wanted to talk, rooting for her. That beat is modest, but it widens the emotional field. Kobuchizawa is not only the girl with the impossible plan. She is someone being watched, misread, and quietly backed by people who may not know what to do with her intensity.

Kimari's role becomes clearer here. She is not asked to solve Antarctica in episode one. She is asked to stop treating her own desire for adventure as a private fantasy and attach it to someone else's real need. That is a smarter opening move than making her instantly heroic. Her help comes through a school call and a changed story. Bureaucratic, slightly messy, human. The sort of small lie that can feel enormous when the alternative is going back to being the girl who almost left.

The ship announcement at Kure Port is the episode's strongest final concrete turn. The icebreaker Shirase being open to the public gives Kobuchizawa's claim a place to go next. The episode does not have to prove Antarctica is reachable yet. It only has to prove the girls can reach the next Saturday, the next port, the next piece of evidence. That is smart opener's math: shrink the impossible until it becomes an appointment.

The best part is how little the episode asks from Kimari at the end. She does not need to transform overnight. She only needs to show up. For a premiere built around a girl who could barely board a train with her own plan, that is enough pressure. Adventure starts to look less like escape and more like accountability.

## The Verdict

"One Million Yen Worth of Youth" is a strong premiere because it gives teenage restlessness a test. Kimari's aimless Tokyo plan could have been cute drift, but Kobuchizawa's missing mother, saved money, and Antarctica goal force the episode to choose direction. The result is funny in its small panic, moving in its blunt grief, and occasionally over-explained when the middle section leans too hard on dialogue.

Even so, the construction is sturdy: bad dream, bad plan, lost money, impossible destination, public ship. As a season opener, it plants two clean engines. Can Kobuchizawa reach Antarctica? How does the one million yen connect her to the group forming around her? The premiere earns those questions by grounding them in work, embarrassment, and a ship the girls can actually visit.

Written by BollyAI, reviewed by our editorial team.

verdict.one_liner: A sharp premiere that turns Kimari's vague escape fantasy into Kobuchizawa's impossible, practical mission toward Antarctica.

episode_reviews.title: A Place Further Than the Universe
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The finale delivers the emotional payoff the series has been building across 12 episodes. The Antarctic setting, the search for what was lost, and the bonds formed during the journey all converge in a sequence that critics and audiences consistently identify as one of the most affecting in contemporary anime.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The email inbox - a scene described by the ANN reviewer as finally delivering the dramatic bite the series had been building toward.

critic_note.text: This episode finally gave me what I wanted most out of this show: a storyline with some genuine dramatic bite.
